In n9, the parenthetical claim that $-a$ has order $p-1$ contradicts the converse assumption that its order is $(p-1)/2$. If the latter order is intended, the argument also uses that $(p-1)/2$ does not divide $(p-1)/p_i$ for odd $p_i$.
The final inference relies on Exercise 4.8, whose statement is not supplied; it appears intended to be the prime-divisor criterion for primitive roots.

nodes.claim: For the forward implication, assume that $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p$.
Factoring $a^{p-1}-1$ and using the order of $a$, the proof obtains $a^{(p-1)/2}\equiv-1\pmod p$.
nodes.text:
As $a^{p-1} \equiv 1(\bmod p), p \mid\left(a^{(p-1) / 2}-1\right)\left(a^{(p-1) / 2}+1\right)$, so $p \mid a^{(p-1) / 2}-1$ or $p \mid$ $a^{(p-1) / 2}+1$. As $a$ is a primitive root modulo $p, a^{(p-1) / 2} \not \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, so

$$

a^{(p-1) / 2} \equiv-1 \quad(\bmod p) .

$$

nodes.claim: Because $(p-1)/2=2t+1$ is odd, the proof obtains $(-a)^{(p-1)/2}\equiv1\pmod p$.
For any positive $n$ with $(-a)^n\equiv1\pmod p$, the primitive-root order of $a$ implies $(p-1)/2$ divides $n$.
nodes.text:
Suppose that $(-a)^n \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, with $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Then $a^{2 n}=(-a)^{2 n} \equiv 1(\bmod p)$, so $p-1\left|2 n, \frac{p-1}{2}\right| n$.

nodes.claim: The exhibited exponent and the divisibility condition yield that $-a$ has order $(p-1)/2$ modulo $p$.
For the converse implication, assume that $-a$ has order $(p-1)/2=2t+1$ modulo $p$.
nodes.text: Conversely, suppose that $-a$ has order $(p-1) / 2=2 t+1$ modulo $p$.

nodes.text: Let $2, p_1, \ldots p_k$ the prime factors of $p-1$, where $p_i$ are odd.

For each odd prime factor $p_i$, the proof uses the even exponent $(p-1)/p_i$ and asserts that $a^{(p-1)/p_i}\not\equiv1\pmod p$, while citing an order of $p-1$ for $-a$.
nodes.text: As $p-1$ is even, $(p-1) / p_i$ is even, so $a^{(p-1) / p_i}=(-a)^{(p-1) / p_i} \not \equiv 1(\bmod p)($ since $-a$ has order $p-1)$.
